    Chapter 16

    Everyday Security: Email, Messaging, Disks, Logins and Money

    🤔 Your 6-digit authenticator code is an HMAC of the clock. Your passkey is a private key inside a chip. And a bitcoin is, at heart, just a signature.

    • ⏱️ ~13 min

    16.1Email#

    Email was designed in the 1970s and 80s for a small, friendly network. Security was bolted on later, in layers.

    Encryption in transit

    • Your device ↔ your email provider: protected by TLS (IMAPS on port 993, SMTP submission on 587/465).
    • Provider ↔ provider: servers try to upgrade their connection with STARTTLS. But it's "opportunistic": if an attacker strips the STARTTLS offer, many servers fall back to plain text. Standards called MTA-STS and DANE let a domain insist on TLS.
    • At rest: your provider can read your email, because it stores it in a form it can decrypt.

    End-to-end encrypted email

    OpenPGP (PGP, GnuPG) S/MIME
    Trust model Web of trust / manual fingerprint checks Certificates from CAs
    Typical users Individuals, journalists, open-source projects Companies, governments
    How it works Hybrid encryption (Chapter 9) + signatures Same idea

    Both have existed since the 1990s and are notoriously hard for ordinary people to use. A famous 1999 study, "Why Johnny Can't Encrypt," found that most participants couldn't correctly sign and encrypt an email with PGP within 90 minutes. Services like Proton Mail use OpenPGP behind the scenes to make it easier.

    🧪 Try it yourself (GnuPG):

    Terminal
    gpg --full-generate-key                          # create your key pair
gpg --armor --export you@example.com > me.asc     # export your PUBLIC key to share
gpg --import bob.asc                              # import a friend's public key
gpg --fingerprint bob@example.com                 # verify it with Bob in person/by phone!

gpg --encrypt --sign --armor -r bob@example.com letter.txt   # → letter.txt.asc
gpg --decrypt letter.txt.asc                                 # Bob decrypts and checks your signature

    Stopping forged senders: SPF, DKIM and DMARC

    The "From:" address in an email is just text; anyone can type anything. Three DNS-based standards fight forgery:

    Standard What it does Crypto?
    SPF The domain publishes a list of servers allowed to send its email No (an allow-list of IP addresses)
    DKIM The sending server signs the message headers and body; the public key is published in DNS ✅ Digital signature
    DMARC The domain tells receivers what to do if SPF/DKIM fail (nothing, quarantine, reject) and where to send reports Policy

    A DKIM signature in an email's headers looks like this (shortened):

    d= is the signing domain, bh= is the hash of the body, b= is the signature. The receiving server fetches the public key from DNS at selector1._domainkey.example.com and verifies it.

    Terminal
    # Look up a domain's DMARC policy
dig +short TXT _dmarc.google.com
# "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:mailauth-reports@google.com"

    In Gmail, open a message → ⋮ → Show original to see SPF: PASS, DKIM: PASS and DMARC: PASS for that message. Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo require bulk senders to use all three.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Email protections

    👍 Situational
    STARTTLS / TLS

    Encryption in transit

    • Automatic, invisible
    • Servers can read your mail
    • Opportunistic: can be stripped
    Best for: Baseline for all mail
    ⚠️ Legacy
    PGP / GnuPG

    End-to-end, web of trust

    • No central authority
    • Strong when used correctly
    • Hard to use; metadata visible
    • No forward secrecy
    Best for: Journalists and developers
    👍 Situational
    S/MIME

    End-to-end with certificates

    • Built into Outlook and Apple Mail
    • Certificate management for everyone
    Best for: Enterprises
    ✅ Use it
    SPF + DKIM + DMARC

    Stop forged senders

    • Blocks spoofing of your domain
    • DKIM signs messages
    • Easy to misconfigure
    • Doesn’t stop look-alike domains
    Best for: Every domain that sends mail

    16.2End-to-end encrypted messaging#

    There's a huge difference between "encrypted" and "end-to-end encrypted":

    With end-to-end encryption (E2EE), even the company running the service, its employees, or anyone who hacks its servers cannot read your messages.

    The Signal Protocol

    The Signal Protocol, designed by Moxie Marlinspike and Trevor Perrin, is the most widely used E2EE design. It powers Signal, WhatsApp (since 2016), Facebook Messenger's default encryption, Google Messages (RCS chats) and others: billions of people.

    Its main ingredients:

    1. Starting a conversation when your friend is offline. Each user uploads a bundle of public keys ("prekeys") to the server in advance. You download your friend's bundle and run a special key agreement (originally X3DH; since 2023 PQXDH, which adds the post-quantum ML-KEM) to derive a shared secret, without your friend being online.
    2. The Double Ratchet: a new key for every message.
      • A symmetric ratchet runs each key through a KDF to produce the next one, then deletes the old one. Like a gear that only turns forward, you can't run it backwards, so a stolen phone doesn't reveal past messages (forward secrecy).
      • A Diffie-Hellman ratchet mixes a fresh key exchange into the chain every time the conversation changes direction. So even if an attacker steals your current keys, they're locked out again after a few messages. This is called post-compromise security, or "self-healing." (In 2025, Signal also began mixing post-quantum keys into this ongoing ratchet.)
    3. Safety numbers. Each conversation has a number (or QR code) derived from both people's identity keys. Comparing it in person defeats a man-in-the-middle, including the server itself.

    Other things worth knowing:

    • Group chats need extra machinery. A newer standard, MLS (Messaging Layer Security, RFC 9420, 2023), handles large groups efficiently.
    • Apple iMessage uses its own protocol, upgraded in 2024 to "PQ3" with post-quantum key exchange.
    • Metadata (who talks to whom, when, how often) is often not protected. Signal works hard to minimize what it stores; other apps collect more.
    • Backups can be the weak point: chat backups to the cloud may not be end-to-end encrypted unless you turn that option on (WhatsApp's encrypted backups, Apple's Advanced Data Protection).
    • ⚠️ Telegram's regular chats are not end-to-end encrypted; only optional "secret chats" are.
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Messaging security

    ✅ Use it
    Signal Protocol

    X3DH/PQXDH + Double Ratchet

    • Forward secrecy and post-compromise security
    • Battle-tested (Signal, WhatsApp)
    • Metadata still partly visible
    • Phone-based identity
    Best for: Private chats
    ✅ Use it
    MLS

    Messaging Layer Security (RFC 9420)

    • Efficient for big groups
    • Interoperable standard
    • Newer; fewer deployments
    Best for: Large group chats
    ⚠️ Legacy
    Server-side encryption only

    “Encrypted” chats the provider can read

    • Cloud sync and search are easy
    • Provider (or a breach) can read everything
    Best for: Non-sensitive chat

    16.3Encrypting data at rest: disks, phones, files and the cloud#

    Data exists in three states, each needing different protection:

    State Example Protection
    In transit Data crossing the network TLS, VPNs, SSH, E2EE
    At rest Data stored on disks, phones, backups, cloud storage Disk/file/database encryption
    In use Data in memory while being processed Hardware "secure enclaves," homomorphic encryption (Chapter 17)

    Full-disk encryption

    If your laptop is stolen, full-disk encryption makes its contents unreadable without your password. Turn it on:

    System Tool Default?
    Windows BitLocker / Device Encryption On by default on many recent PCs
    macOS FileVault Prompted at setup
    Linux LUKS (often via the installer) Optional at install
    iPhone / iPad Data Protection ✅ Always on with a passcode
    Android File-Based Encryption ✅ On by default on modern phones

    Disks are encrypted with AES in XTS mode, designed for storage. There's also a clever key hierarchy:

    Because of this layering, changing your password doesn't require re-encrypting the whole disk; only the small wrapped master key changes. And the security chip makes a short PIN surprisingly strong. On an iPhone, the passcode is mixed with a unique hardware key that can't be extracted, so guesses can only be made on that phone, with growing delays (and an optional wipe after 10 failures).

    ⚠️ Watch out:

    • Save your recovery key somewhere safe. Without it, a forgotten password can mean the data is gone forever. That's the point of encryption.
    • Disk encryption protects a device that's off (or locked). While you're logged in, the data is readable by anything running on the computer.

    Files, archives and the cloud

    • For individual files: age, GnuPG, VeraCrypt containers, or 7-Zip with AES-256. ⚠️ Avoid the old "ZipCrypto" encryption in ZIP files; it's weak.
    • Cloud storage is usually encrypted at rest by the provider with the provider's keys. That protects against stolen hard drives in a data center, but not against the provider itself or someone with access to its systems. Client-side or end-to-end encrypted storage (Apple's Advanced Data Protection, Proton Drive, tools like Cryptomator) means only you hold the keys.
    • Crypto-shredding: to delete encrypted data permanently, delete its key. Without the key, the ciphertext is just noise. Cloud providers use this to erase data reliably.
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Data-at-rest encryption

    ✅ Use it
    Full-disk encryption

    BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS

    • Protects a lost or stolen laptop
    • Transparent once unlocked
    • No protection while the device is on and unlocked
    • Recovery key must be stored safely
    Best for: Every laptop and phone
    ✅ Use it
    File / archive encryption

    age, GnuPG, encrypted ZIP

    • Protects files when shared or backed up
    • Weak passwords; old ZIP crypto is weak
    Best for: Sending or archiving files
    ✅ Use it
    Cloud E2EE

    You hold the keys

    • Provider can’t read your data
    • Lose the key, lose the data
    • Fewer server-side features
    Best for: Sensitive cloud backups
    ✔ section read

    16.4Logging in: passwords, 2FA codes and passkeys#

    There are three kinds of authentication factor:

    • Something you know: a password or PIN.
    • Something you have: a phone, a security key.
    • Something you are: a fingerprint, your face.

    Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two or more.

    SMS codes

    Better than nothing, but weak: attackers can talk a mobile carrier into moving your number to their SIM card ("SIM swapping"), and codes can be phished.

    Authenticator app codes (TOTP)

    The 6-digit codes in Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password and similar apps use TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password, RFC 6238). It's an HMAC (Chapter 7) of the current time:

    1. When you set up 2FA, the website shows a QR code containing a shared secret, like otpauth://totp/Example:alice?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=Example.
    2. Your app and the website both store that secret.
    3. Every 30 seconds, both compute HMAC-SHA1(secret, current_time ÷ 30) and shorten the result to 6 digits.
    4. If your code matches the server's, you're in.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python, a complete TOTP generator in a dozen lines):

    Python
    import hmac, hashlib, struct, time, base64

def totp(secret: bytes, for_time: int, digits=6, step=30):
    counter = for_time // step                                  # which 30-second window
    mac = hmac.new(secret, struct.pack(">Q", counter), hashlib.sha1).digest()
    offset = mac[-1] & 0x0F                                     # "dynamic truncation"
    code = (struct.unpack(">I", mac[offset:offset+4])[0] & 0x7FFFFFFF) % (10 ** digits)
    return str(code).zfill(digits)

# Official test vector from RFC 6238: secret "12345678901234567890", time 59 → 94287082
print(totp(b"12345678901234567890", 59, digits=8))   # 94287082

# The secret from the QR code above (Base32-encoded). Add it to an authenticator
# app manually and compare: the codes will match.
secret = base64.b32decode("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP")
print(totp(secret, int(time.time())))

    ⚠️ TOTP codes can still be phished: a fake login page can ask for your code and use it on the real site within seconds.

    Push notifications and "MFA fatigue"

    "Approve this sign-in?" prompts are convenient, but attackers who have your password can spam you with prompts until you tap "Approve" by mistake or out of annoyance. 📜 This "MFA fatigue" trick was used in a 2022 breach of Uber. Modern apps add number matching (type the number shown on the login screen) to counter it.

    Passkeys: public-key cryptography replaces passwords

    Passkeys (built on the FIDO2 / WebAuthn standards) replace passwords entirely with a key pair:

    Why passkeys are a big improvement:

    • Phishing-resistant: the browser includes the real website's domain in what gets signed, and a passkey created for bank.example simply won't be offered to bank-example-login.com. A fake site gets nothing useful.
    • Nothing to steal from the server: the website stores only public keys. A database breach reveals nothing an attacker can log in with.
    • Nothing to remember or reuse.
    • Your fingerprint or face never leaves your device. It only unlocks the private key locally.

    Passkeys can sync between your devices through Apple's iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager or password managers (end-to-end encrypted), or live on a hardware security key like a YubiKey.

    Method Phishing-resistant? Server breach exposes it? Convenience
    Password only ❌ ⚠️ Hashes (crackable if weak) Must remember
    Password + SMS ❌ ⚠️ Wait for SMS
    Password + TOTP app ❌ ⚠️ Type a code
    Password + push with number matching ⚠️ Better ⚠️ Tap and type
    Passkey / security key ✅ ✅ No: only public keys stored Touch or glance

    "Sign in with Google/Apple/Microsoft" (single sign-on) uses standards called OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect: the identity provider authenticates you and hands the website a signed token stating who you are, usually a JWT.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…

    Second factors and logins

    ⚠️ Legacy
    SMS codes

    Text message

    • Works on any phone
    • Better than no 2FA
    • SIM swapping and SS7 interception
    • Phishable
    Best for: Last resort
    👍 Situational
    TOTP app

    HMAC of the time

    • Offline; free; standard (RFC 6238)
    • Phishable in real time
    • Shared secret stored on the server
    Best for: Good default 2FA
    👍 Situational
    Push approval

    Tap “Approve”

    • Convenient
    • MFA fatigue: users approve spam prompts
    Best for: With number matching
    ✅ Use it
    Passkeys / security keys

    WebAuthn public-key login

    • Phishing-resistant (domain-bound)
    • Nothing secret stored on the server
    • Fast to use
    • Account recovery planning needed
    • Cross-device sync depends on ecosystem
    Best for: Everything that supports them

    16.5Web tokens: JWTs#

    A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, signed piece of data that a server gives you after login. You send it back with each request to prove who you are. It has three Base64url-encoded parts separated by dots:

    If Alice edits the payload to "admin":true, the signature no longer matches and the server rejects the token.

    ⚠️ The most important JWT fact: signed is not encrypted. Anyone can decode the payload. Never put secrets in it:

    Python
    import base64
payload = "eyJzdWIiOiJhbGljZSIsImFkbWluIjpmYWxzZSwiZXhwIjoxNzk4NzYxNjAwfQ"
print(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload + "=" * (-len(payload) % 4)))
# b'{"sub":"alice","admin":false,"exp":1798761600}'

    (Paste any JWT into a decoder like jwt.io to see this, but never paste real production tokens into websites.)

    alg Meaning
    HS256 HMAC-SHA256 with a shared secret (the server that creates tokens also verifies them)
    RS256 / PS256 RSA signature (others can verify with the public key)
    ES256 ECDSA P-256 signature
    EdDSA Ed25519 signature

    Classic JWT mistakes:

    • 📜 "alg": "none": some libraries once accepted tokens that declared "no signature," letting attackers forge any token. Always enforce the expected algorithm on the server.
    • Algorithm confusion: tricking a server that expects RS256 into treating its public key as an HS256 secret.
    • Weak HS256 secrets: short secrets can be brute-forced offline from a single token. Use at least 32 random bytes.
    • No expiry: always set exp and keep lifetimes short.
    • If you need the contents hidden, use JWE (JSON Web Encryption).
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    JWT signing algorithms

    👍 Situational
    HS256

    HMAC-SHA256

    • Tiny and fast
    • Every verifier can also forge
    • Weak secrets can be brute-forced
    Best for: One service issuing and verifying
    👍 Situational
    RS256 / PS256

    RSA signatures

    • Public verification; very widespread
    • Large tokens
    • Algorithm-confusion pitfalls
    Best for: Identity providers
    ✅ Use it
    ES256 / EdDSA

    ECDSA P-256 / Ed25519

    • Small tokens; public verification
    • ES256 needs good nonces (libraries handle it)
    Best for: Modern APIs
    ❌ Avoid
    alg: none

    “No signature”

    • None
    • Anyone can forge any token
    Best for: Reject it, always
    ✔ section read

    16.6Cryptocurrency and blockchains#

    "Crypto" in the news usually means cryptocurrency. It isn't the same thing as cryptography, but it's built entirely from the tools in this guide. (This section explains the technology only; it isn't financial advice.)

    Bitcoin's ingredients:

    Concept Crypto tool Chapter
    Your wallet's private key A random 256-bit number 4
    Your public key k × G on the secp256k1 elliptic curve 9
    Your address A hash of your public key (SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160), encoded as text 6
    Spending coins Signing a transaction with your private key (ECDSA, or Schnorr since 2021) 11
    Blocks chained together Each block contains the hash of the previous one 6
    All transactions in a block Summarized by a Merkle root 6
    Mining (proof of work) Searching for a number that makes the block's double-SHA-256 hash start with many zeros 6

    Proof of work is a lottery: miners repeatedly change a number (the nonce) and hash the block until, by luck, the hash falls below a target. It takes enormous computing power to win, which is what makes rewriting history impractical. Ethereum switched in 2022 to proof of stake, which uses signatures from participants who lock up funds instead of mining.

    Seed phrases. Wallets show you 12 or 24 words (a standard called BIP-39). Those words encode the master random secret from which all your keys are derived.

    ⚠️ Anyone who has your seed phrase has your money. No bank, no password reset, no undo. Never type it into a website, never share it with "support staff," never store it as a photo in the cloud. "Not your keys, not your coins": if an exchange holds the keys for you, you're trusting the exchange.

    Lost keys mean lost funds forever. Researchers estimate that millions of bitcoins are permanently inaccessible because their owners lost their keys.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Blockchain building blocks

    💡 Concept
    Hash-chained blocks

    Each block holds the previous hash

    • Tamper-evident history
    • Doesn’t stop a majority of miners/validators
    Best for: Public ledgers, audit logs
    💡 Concept
    Proof of work

    Find a hash below a target

    • Permissionless and simple
    • Enormous energy use
    Best for: Bitcoin
    💡 Concept
    Proof of stake

    Validators lock up coins

    • ~99.9% less energy
    • More complex security assumptions
    Best for: Ethereum since 2022
    💡 Concept
    Wallet = private key

    secp256k1 signatures

    • You truly own your funds
    • Lose the key, lose the money; no undo
    Best for: Use hardware wallets + backups

    16.7Software supply chain: code signing and secure updates#

    How do you know an app or update really comes from its developer, and wasn't modified along the way?

    • Code signing: developers sign their software (Chapter 11). Your operating system checks the signature before running it: macOS Gatekeeper and notarization, Windows SmartScreen and Authenticode, Android's APK signature checks, iOS's App Store signatures.
    • Secure Boot: a chain of trust at startup. The firmware checks the bootloader's signature, the bootloader checks the operating system's, and so on. A TPM chip can record ("measure") each step so the system can prove it booted cleanly.
    • Package managers: Linux repositories sign their package lists with GPG. Newer systems like Sigstore let developers sign software with short-lived certificates tied to their login identity, and record every signature in a public transparency log (like Certificate Transparency for software).
    • Git commit signing: prove who wrote a commit. With an SSH key:
    Terminal
    git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git commit -m "Signed commit"          # GitHub/GitLab show a "Verified" badge

    📜 SolarWinds (2020): attackers broke into a software company's build system and inserted malware into a product update. The update was then legitimately signed and installed by thousands of organizations, including government agencies. Lesson: a signature proves who shipped the code, not that the code is safe.

    📜 The xz backdoor (2024): over about two years, someone using the name "Jia Tan" gained the trust of the maintainer of xz, a compression library used throughout Linux, and slipped in a hidden backdoor that targeted SSH servers. It was discovered by chance, just before reaching major Linux releases, by a Microsoft engineer, Andres Freund, who noticed SSH logins taking about half a second longer than usual. Lesson: supply-chain security is about people and processes as much as cryptography.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Supply-chain protections

    ✅ Use it
    Code signing

    Sign releases and updates

    • Users know who published it
    • Tampered updates fail verification
    • Stolen signing keys sign malware too
    Best for: All software distribution
    ✅ Use it
    Sigstore / transparency

    Keyless signing + public logs

    • No long-lived keys to steal
    • Public audit trail
    • Depends on identity providers
    Best for: Open-source packages
    ✅ Use it
    Reproducible builds

    Anyone can rebuild bit-for-bit

    • Catches compromised build servers
    • Hard to achieve
    Best for: Critical projects
